Occurrences.AttributionNote: Orthodox Continuation of the Lamp (續燈正統), in Zhu'an Shigui's section: asked about the National Teacher calling his attendant three times, Zhu'an says a drum is beaten to make a monkey perform and the monkey runs when the drum breaks.

Senses.Explanation: A monkey becomes a recurring answer and acted image in Chan records. Huangbo Xiyun answers a question about Chan, 'a monkey climbs a tree, its tail tumbling over its head' (猢猻上樹尾連顛). Deshan Yuanmi tethers the monkey to a pillar before the buddha appears and puts it into a cloth bag afterward; Poshan Haiming separately answers that a monkey enters a cloth bag. Doushuai Congyue makes two monkeys hang by four tails, while Zhu'an Shigui has a drum-beaten monkey run away when the drum breaks. The Chan-specific bend is this repeated placement of the animal in public answers, paired before-and-after sayings, and impossible stage-scenes; the entry does not assign a hidden meaning to those actions.

Senses.Explanation: To put on the play when the occasion appears is to have the props ready and perform responsively when a situation calls for it. Shiyu Mingfang applies the phrase to carrying a fly-whisk into public performance and criticizes the muddy spectacle it produced. Yuan'an Feng, Buhui, Baiyu Si, and Feiyin Tongrong instead use it for responsive teaching action: a no-stringed lute, a no-hole flute, a whisk raised at the right point, or free movement amid the ten directions. The phrase therefore keeps its theatrical scene while Chan records test whether the performance is timely and capable or merely showmanship.

SearchAliases: meet a patriarch kill the patriarch
Senses.Explanation: “Meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch” belongs to Linji’s enumerated formula of killing whatever is encountered, and later masters quote that wording as a sharp inherited command. Literally, "meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch" . Linji's surviving record places it inside a five-member roster: "meet buddha, kill buddha; meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch; meet an arhat, kill the arhat; meet parents, kill parents; meet kin, kill kin" . This is the Chan bend: the honored religious and familial titles become the grammatical objects of the same repeated verb, and later masters preserve, question, and redeploy that severe roster. A successor record explicitly asks why a good teacher would want to kill people after quoting the three religious members, without supplying a prose gloss. Later uses attach the phrase to a sharp sword, place it opposite "carry the infant and encourage the child" in a contrast about grandmotherly kindness, or quote it in a New Year's address before comments on lineage descent. The records use killing language literally in the formula but do not record bodily killings in these deployments; this entry adds no symbolic object behind the named roster.
